Online marketplace eBay has imposed new restrictions on listings of radio transmitting equipment in response to new FCC rules that took effect this week, but responded to ARRL that its new policy will not apply to gear that operates exclusively on amateur radio frequencies. The FCC’s rules are intended to use its equipment authorization program to protect against “national security threats to the communications supply chain” and cover a wide variety of products.

In its Third Report and Order issued on July 23, 2026, the Commission makes clear that online marketplaces share in the legal responsibility to assure that unauthorized RF devices are not offered for sale on their platforms. The rules took effect on October 13. Moving forward, equipment subject to FCC authorization must have its FCC ID number submitted to the marketplace and posted with its listing. There are exemptions for posts already online, “small sellers,” and used equipment, but initial messages to sellers from eBay suggested that an FCC ID would be required in order to post a listing for any equipment that transmits RF energy.

In response to a request from ARRL for a clarification relating to amateur radio equipment that does not require FCC authorization, an eBay spokesperson provided the following statement:

eBay allows the sale of devices capable of operating only on frequencies that the FCC has allocated for use by Amateur Radio Service licensees. As these devices do not require FCC equipment authorization, FCC IDs will not be required for these listings as an amateur licensee may use his or her license to operate such radios.
However, two-way VHF/UHF radio equipment capable of operating outside of the amateur frequency bands cannot be imported, advertised, sold, or operated within the United States, including on eBay, without an FCC equipment certification.
If eBay inadvertently takes action against listings for devices that don't require FCC IDs and are otherwise authorized, the affected seller should inform eBay and we will assess whether to remove restrictions from the listing.

It should be emphasized that the FCC did not change its underlying equipment authorization rules. Amateur radio equipment, except for commercial HF amplifiers, continues to not require FCC authorization.

The Radio Club of America has brought together both wireless industry

professionals and amateur radio operators for more than 100 years. Each year, it bestows prestigious awards and elevates several members to RCA Fellows. This year, as always, many of those on the list are hams. The award recipients include Dr. Charles C. Counselman, III, W1HIS, who developed technology for making highly accurate GPS positioning widely available; Jay Adrick, K8CJY, who helped develop digital television and serves as Board President of the National Voice of America Museum of Broadcasting; inventor Charles Kirmuss, WØCBK, who developed digital video and audio recording systems for public safety; Carole Perry Young Professional Award winner and electrical engineer Audrey McElroy, KM4BUN, a longtime proponent of youth in amateur radio; Dr. Ajay Poddar, AC2KG, an internationally-recognized leader in radio science and engineering; Dr. Henry Richter, W6VZA (SK), who developed the communications system for Explorer 1, the first US Earth satellite; and Anthony Rizi, NR1Z, a military and cybersecurity professional and college professor who is also active in ARISS, the Amateur Radio on the International Space Station program.

This year’s class of RCA Fellows include amateurs Rachel Jones, KO4HLC; Geoffrey Mendenhall, W8GNM; Nick Pennance, N1CKP, and Dominic “Nick” Tusa, K5EF. The award winners and new Fellows will be formally recognized at RCA’s 2026 Technical Symposium and Awards Banquet in New York City on November 21. Visit the club’s website for a complete list of awardees and their biographies.

Back in the earliest days of the internet, a whole block of IP (internet

protocol) addresses — beginning with 44 — was set aside for amateur radio use. Most of that block of addresses is still there and is managed by ARDC, Amateur Radio Digital Communications. In December of 2025, ARDC launched 44Net Connect, a service intended to make it easy for hams to begin using 44Net addresses for such things as experimenting with digital modes, improving repeater infrastructure, setting up a home lab, and more. In the ensuing months, more than 2000 users have signed up and ARDC is now expanding access by doubling its number of “points of presence,” or “PoPs” around the world, adding new ones in Chicago, Los Angeles, and Sydney, Australia (current ones are in Frankfurt, Toronto, and Dallas). A PoP is a physical access point that connects different networks. “The additional PoPs will expand network capacity and bring nodes closer to users in different parts of the world,” explained Rebecca Key, KO4KVG, ARDC’s Communications Manager. “This can shorten the distance data travels, reducing latency, and improving the overall experience.”

“44Net Connect gives licensed hams a simpler way to get a static 44Net IP address without a complicated setup,” adds Key. “We’re seeing it used for everything from personal tinkering to club projects, education, and EmComm.”

You can find more information about 44Net Connect, including how to get started, in ARDC’s introductory blog post.

Mel Parkes, NM7P, has resigned as Vice Director of the ARRL Rocky Mountain Division, effective October 10, 2026. Parkes was elected in 2025 to a three-year term that began January 1, 2026. He cited health and personal reasons for his resignation.

Previously, Parkes served as Utah Section Manager for 22 years, from 1999 until 2021.

ARRL President Rick Roderick, K5UR, has appointed Ed James, KA8JMW, of Edgewood, New Mexico, to be the new Vice Director, serving the remainder of Parkes’ term, which runs through December 31, 2028. An ARRL Life Member, James has served in multiple ARRL Field Organization positions, including Section Manager of New Mexico.

ARRL is governed by an all-volunteer Board of Directors. Elections are held annually for five of ARRL’s 15 Divisions, with Directors and Vice Directors serving 3-year terms.

The Dog Day Radio Amateur Radio Club, KØDOG, is back on the air from the 1st through the 7th of November. In observance of International Dog Day in August, the club’s monthlong activities were all about the rescue and responsible care of dogs. In November, operators are calling CQ for one week in recognition of the selfless work of the volunteers, rescuers, veterinarians, shelter staffers and other supporters of animals in need of loving and responsible homes. The event coincides with National Animal Shelter Appreciation Week created by the Humane Society of the US. Listen for KØDOG on the HF bands, using CW and SSB. Share your own stories as adopters, foster caregivers and rescue workers. QSL cards are available for all confirmed contacts and SWLs who send an SASE. Visit KØDOG on QRZ.com to learn how you can donate professional services, funds, clean towels and sheets, or some toys and food.

The Nashua Area Radio Society, an ARRL Affiliated Club, will be holding its next online Ham Bootcamp on Saturday November 14th from 10 AM to 6 PM Eastern time. Ham Bootcamp is an online, interactive program to help new, inactive, and prospective hams learn the skills that they need to get on the air. The morning sessions are all about VHF and the afternoon sessions focus on HF. There is no fee to attend Ham Bootcamp. Advance registration is requested. Questions may be emailed to bootcamp@n1fd.org.

The 21st annual ARRL Online Auction gets under way tomorrow, October 16, and runs through October 22, with more than 200 items up for bid. The auction preview is already open. This year’s selection includes gear from QST “Product Review” articles, vintage books, pre-owned equipment, signed original sketches by Salty Walt Hudson, K4OGO, from Salty Walt’s Portable Antenna Sketchbook, and four popular mystery boxes contributed by the ARRL Lab team. Featured equipment includes the Icom IC-PW2 solid-state amplifier, Alinco DR-CS10HT 2-meter FM transceiver, and Elecraft KH1 QRP transceiver with the Edgewood package, along with many other items.

Proceeds from the annual auction benefit ARRL education programs, including efforts to license new hams, provide continuing technical and operating education, and develop instructional materials.

All bidders must register on the auction website at arrl.auctionanything.com. Your ARRL account username and password will not work on the auction site. If you have participated in a previous ARRL Online Auction, you may use your existing auction login information. If you have forgotten your auction User ID or password, click the Help tab for instructions. Before bidding, be sure your mailing address and other account information are up to date.

Nominations are open for the 2027 CWOps Award for Advancing the Art of CW. The purpose of the award is to recognize individuals, groups, and organizations that have made the greatest contribution(s) toward advancing the art or practice of radio communications by Morse code. Candidates for the award may be one or more of the following: Authors of publications related to CW; CW recruiters, trainers, mentors, coaches and instructors; public advocates of CW; organizers of CW activities; designers and inventors who advance the art or practice of CW, and other contributors to the art or practice of CW. The award is not limited to amateur radio operators or their organizations.

Nominations may be made by anyone and must include the nominee’s name, call sign (if applicable), and complete contact information; nominator’s name and contact information, and a detailed explanation supporting the nominee’s qualifications for recognition. Nominations must be emailed by February 15, 2027, to awards@cwops.org with a copy to secretary@cwops.org. The winner will be recognized with a plaque at the 2027 Dayton Hamvention®.

Six new amateur radio satellites built by three different AMSAT organizations were launched into orbit on October 1, riding aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission. The AMSAT News Service reports that the group includes three PocketQubes from AMSAT-DL in Germany, two satellites from AMSAT-EA in Spain, and another PocketQube from AMSAT Nepal. The spacecraft traveled aboard OSSIE-D, the first orbital transfer vehicle developed by Spanish space transportation company UARX Space. Following separation from the Falcon 9 upper stage, OSSIE-D began deploying its collection of small satellites, giving the worldwide AMSAT community a particularly strong presence on the mission.

The AMSAT-DL “PocketQubes” are satellites measuring just 5 centimeters on each side, intended to promote amateur radio and space technology through open-source communications, telemetry, and other experiments. AMSAT-EA’s two satellites offer voice communication capabilities. HADES-E2 carries a repeater with a 145.925 MHz uplink and 436.888 MHz downlink, while HADES-L features a 10-meter uplink, on 29.472 MHz USB, with an FM downlink on 436.665 MHz. AMSAT Nepal’s SanoSat-2, also a 5-centimeter PocketQube, carries a camera capable of transmitting images as SSDV packets using GFSK modulation, allowing amateurs to receive and reconstruct imagery from orbit. SanoSat-2 can also operate as a digital store-and-forward repeater through which amateur operators can upload messages for later transmission.

ARRL member and Amateur Extra Class operator Brian Daly, WB7OML, has been reappointed to both the FCC's Communications Security, Reliability and Interoperability Council (CSRIC) and the Technological Advisory Council (TAC). He has also been selected to continue serving as Co-Lead of the TAC Emerging Wireless Broadband Working Group, which is examining technologies and policies that will influence the future of wireless broadband communications. Daly is an AT&T Fellow and Radio Club of America Fellow. The appointments place him among a select group of experts advising the FCC on issues ranging from communications security and network resilience to emerging wireless technologies and future spectrum needs. Daly says his continued service reflects the longstanding tradition of amateur radio operators contributing technical expertise, innovation, and public service at the highest levels of communications policy and technology development.

Jamboree on the Air (JOTA) is this weekend, October 17 and 18, and as we’ve been reporting, radio scouting groups are preparing to help Scouts around the world get on the air. ARRL Puerto Rico Section Public Information Coordinator Angel Santana, WP3GW, reports that multiple amateur radio groups on the island will be working with Scouts from nearly 20 different troops to help them make radio contacts and earn their radio merit badges. According to Santana, this is Puerto Rico’s largest-ever JOTA activation.

ARRL member Carol Laferty Dantzler, K4SAF, of Clearfield, Kentucky, was presented with a plaque on September 26 in recognition of her 69 years as a licensed amateur radio operator. Carol has been licensed since 1957. She has earned ARRL’s 5-Band DXCC and 5-Band Worked All States awards, as well as the Young Ladies Radio League’s Worked All States - YL award. Carol is also an ARRL card-checker for Kentucky. She was presented with the plaque at the Paintsville, Kentucky, Hamfest by ARRL Kentucky Section Manager Bob Selbrede, K6ZZ.

Look for improved propagation on the upper HF bands, as both the sunspot numbers and 10.7-centimeter radio flux remain near or above 100. According to NOAA’s Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC), the increase in activity is being fueled primarily by sunspot Region 4551, which is described as the largest and most complex of six sunspot regions currently visible on the surface of the Sun. Mostly quiet geomagnetic conditions are expected as well, with some disturbances possible late next week.

The Australian Space Weather Forecasting Centre predicts mostly normal HF propagation conditions worldwide.

The W3LPL Propagation Forecast from the Daily DX is predicting significantly improved DX conditions on 10 and 12 meters for as many as the next 10 days, with excellent conditions on 17, 15, and 20 meters as well. DX openings on 30 meters should begin in late afternoon each day, followed by 40 meters around an hour before sunset, and 80 meters just after sunset.

Keep listening for DXpeditions and other activity from rare DX locations as stations get tuned up for the CQ World Wide SSB DX Contest on October 24 and 25.

Predicted 10.7-centimeter solar flux: Oct 15, 105; Oct 16, 100; Oct 17-18, 95; Oct 19-20, 100; Oct 21, 105, Oct 22, 100. (Source: NOAA SWPC)

Share your reports and observations. Send your tips, questions, or comments to w2vu@arrl.org.

Online marketplace eBay has imposed new restrictions on listings of radio transmitting equipment in response to new FCC rules that took effect this week, but responded to ARRL that its new policy will not apply to gear that operates exclusively on amateur radio frequencies. The FCC’s rules are intended to use its equipment authorization program to protect against “national security threats to the communications supply chain” and cover a wide variety of products.
https://www.arrl.org/img/newsletter/95649b8b872476252d0e0b536/images/707e8447-235c-7dae-75a7-b8b06d4041b8.jpg

In its Third Report and Order issued on July 23, 2026, the Commission makes clear that online marketplaces share in the legal responsibility to assure that unauthorized RF devices are not offered for sale on their platforms. The rules took effect on October 13. Moving forward, equipment subject to FCC authorization must have its FCC ID number submitted to the marketplace and posted with its listing. There are exemptions for posts already online, “small sellers,” and used equipment, but initial messages to sellers from eBay suggested that an FCC ID would be required in order to post a listing for any equipment that transmits RF energy.
In response to a request from ARRL for a clarification relating to amateur radio equipment that does not require FCC authorization, an eBay spokesperson provided the following statement:

eBay allows the sale of devices capable of operating only on frequencies that the FCC has allocated for use by Amateur Radio Service licensees. As these devices do not require FCC equipment authorization, FCC IDs will not be required for these listings as an amateur licensee may use his or her license to operate such radios.
However, two-way VHF/UHF radio equipment capable of operating outside of the amateur frequency bands cannot be imported, advertised, sold, or operated within the United States, including on eBay, without an FCC equipment certification.
If eBay inadvertently takes action against listings for devices that don't require FCC IDs and are otherwise authorized, the affected seller should inform eBay and we will assess whether to remove restrictions from the listing.

It should be emphasized that the FCC did not change its underlying equipment authorization rules. Amateur radio equipment, except for commercial HF amplifiers, continues to not require FCC authorization.

https://www.arrl.org/img/newsletter/95649b8b872476252d0e0b536/images/bd04c1a8-61f0-5921-4ae4-22bb4f3e40b6.jpg

protocol) addresses — beginning with 44 — was set aside for amateur radio use. Most of that block of addresses is still there and is managed by ARDC, Amateur Radio Digital Communications. In December of 2025, ARDC launched 44Net Connect, a service intended to make it easy for hams to begin using 44Net addresses for such things as experimenting with digital modes, improving repeater infrastructure, setting up a home lab, and more. In the ensuing months, more than 2000 users have signed up and ARDC is now expanding access by doubling its number of “points of presence,” or “PoPs” around the world, adding new ones in Chicago, Los Angeles, and Sydney, Australia (current ones are in Frankfurt, Toronto, and Dallas). A PoP is a physical access point that connects different networks. “The additional PoPs will expand network capacity and bring nodes closer to users in different parts of the world,” explained Rebecca Key, KO4KVG, ARDC’s Communications Manager. “This can shorten the distance data travels, reducing latency, and improving the overall experience.”

“44Net Connect gives licensed hams a simpler way to get a static 44Net IP address without a complicated setup,” adds Key. “We’re seeing it used for everything from personal tinkering to club projects, education, and EmComm.”

Six new amateur radio satellites built by three different AMSAT organizations were launched into orbit on October 1, riding aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission. The AMSAT News Service reports that the group includes three PocketQubes from AMSAT-DL in Germany, two satellites from AMSAT-EA in Spain, and another PocketQube from AMSAT Nepal. The spacecraft traveled aboard OSSIE-D, the first orbital transfer vehicle developed by Spanish space transportation company UARX Space. Following separation from the Falcon 9 upper stage, OSSIE-D began deploying its collection of small satellites, giving the worldwide AMSAT community a particularly strong presence on the mission.

The AMSAT-DL “PocketQubes” are satellites measuring just 5 centimeters on each side, intended to promote amateur radio and space technology through open-source communications, telemetry, and other experiments. AMSAT-EA’s two satellites offer voice communication capabilities. HADES-E2 carries a repeater with a 145.925 MHz uplink and 436.888 MHz downlink, while HADES-L features a 10-meter uplink, on 29.472 MHz USB, with an FM downlink on 436.665 MHz. AMSAT Nepal’s SanoSat-2, also a 5-centimeter PocketQube, carries a camera capable of transmitting images as SSDV packets using GFSK modulation, allowing amateurs to receive and reconstruct imagery from orbit. SanoSat-2 can also operate as a digital store-and-forward repeater through which amateur operators can upload messages for later transmission.

items.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein
items.author: gmays
items.summary: Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with
items.text:
Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area.

FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world.

The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License.

Try it in the BFL API · Download the weights

Leading open weights quality with fewer parameters

In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters.

Parameter counts are for the image generator, as each publisher reports them; text encoders are not counted. Krea 2 does not support image editing and is not included in the image editing comparison.

FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI.

The base checkpoint is built for fine-tuning: Diffusers and Ostris's AI Toolkit support LoRA training from day one, and NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel ships recipes that work directly from the released checkpoints.

For even faster production workloads that need lower latency, we also work with teams on specific customizations that get you there. Get in touch.

On the speed–quality frontier

FLUX 3 Image Klein also extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier. Through the BFL API, it delivers lower latency than Qwen-Image 2.1, FLUX.2 [pro], Ideogram V4.5 and Krea 2, and the highest rating at its latency and above. In the charts below, the violet line traces the highest rating available at each latency and the gray line shows the previous frontier.

Latency is measured end to end, from request submission to the finished 1 MP image, including queueing. FLUX 3 Image Klein was timed on our servers. Other models were timed from the client, which includes polling and network time. Krea 2 was timed on its Medium tier; its Large tier took 31.1 seconds for text-to-image.

Get started

FLUX 3 Image Klein is available today as open weights and through the BFL API.

Try it

BFL API: the distilled model is available as flux-3-image-klein, with prompt upsampling and pixel restoration, which preserves unedited regions of an image exactly. Pricing starts at $0.009 per 1K image.

Playground or Hugging Face.

Try it out on Hugging Face Spaces.

LoRA training with Ostris's AI Toolkit and recipes in NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel.

Trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform, serving through NVIDIA TensorRT LLM, vLLM-Omni and SGLang Diffusion.

On NVIDIA GB300, the distilled model generates a 1MP image in under 0.6 seconds in NVFP4. Serving a LoRA adds around 5% to generation time.

License

The weights are available under the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and companies with annual revenue under $5M, alongside research and non-commercial use. Larger organizations can deploy commercially through our self-hosted licensing options or API.

Safety

In an effort to make AI technology both open and safe, we implement multiple safeguards throughout the model development lifecycle to combat misuse. These include dataset filters during pre-training to limit exposure to harmful content, and targeted fine-tuning during post-training to suppress harmful behaviors, making it progressively harder to elicit harmful content. Ahead of the release, the FLUX 3 Image Klein checkpoints were rigorously red teamed internally and evaluated by our external safety partner Cinder, demonstrating substantially fewer vulnerabilities than other popular open weights models. More on our safety methodology is available here.

FLUX 3 Image Klein is the second open weights release from the FLUX 3 family, following FLUX 3 Action. More will follow.

Introduction

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is a minor update to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, delivering substantial improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic tasks, and visual benchmarks. Alongside these gains, the model reduces task execution time and output length, enabling users to complete tasks faster and at lower cost and advancing the performance–cost Pareto frontier across multiple agent harnesses.

Prompt Encoding

This release does not include a Jinja-format chat template. The encoding folder contains a self-contained Python reference implementation (encoding.py) with test cases for multi-turn conversations, tool calling, thinking mode, numeric reasoning effort, mid-conversation system messages, and interleaved image content.

For production use, we additionally release deepseek-recipe, a set of Rust libraries with Python bindings that provides the same prompt format as a maintained, protocol-aware toolkit. It converts Messages, Chat Completions, and Responses API requests into the Conversation format, encodes them into DeepSeek V4 and V4.1 prompts or token IDs, and parses model output back into complete or streamed responses — covering thinking, tool calls, images, and generation settings. Model inference, tool execution, and HTTP transport are left to the caller.

items.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
items.author: pretext
items.summary: Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight
items.text:
Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated.

This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). Read the full paper on arXiv.

Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in qubits, which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as superposition—which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.

The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer.

Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.

In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)

Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits.1

These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classical algorithms, so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.

For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. A new reversible algorithm

Designing a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs.

The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result. The only way to discard information is to “uncompute” it by running the computation that created it in reverse, at the cost of additional gates. Both of these constraints make quantum circuits far more expensive, in both runtime and qubits, than their classical counterparts.

This constraint forces a difficult trade-off between space (i.e., qubits) and time. At one extreme, a quantum circuit can uncompute intermediate results as soon as they have been used. This frees up qubits, but if those same results are needed again later, the circuit must recompute them, which adds gates and increases the runtime. At the other extreme, the circuit can retain intermediate results until they’re no longer needed. This avoids repeating work, but it can require many more qubits.

This is what makes quantum circuit design an especially interesting test of Claude’s capabilities. The circuits can be written as ordinary code, but improving them requires the model to reason under a set of constraints quite unlike those of ordinary programming.

A hard first test: modular inversion

The first task we gave Claude was point addition, a rule for combining two points on a mathematical curve (an elliptic curve) to produce a third. Point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves: given a starting point and the result of adding it to itself n times, find n. For large curves, ordinary computers can’t solve this problem in any reasonable amount of time, but a sufficiently large quantum computer could.

These algorithms perform point addition many times over, including in reverse, and these additions account for most of their qubit and runtime costs. Problems like this—easy to compute, extremely hard to reverse—were among the first where quantum computers were shown to offer an exponential speedup over ordinary ones. For these reasons, point addition has become one of the field’s standard benchmarks. This made it a demanding test for Claude. So, we asked it to map out how few qubits, as well as how few gates, point addition really needs.

We gave Claude a one-paragraph brief. It explained the mathematical rule for point addition, and how the evaluator would check each proposed circuit for correctness and score it on the number of qubits and gates it used. It also instructed Claude to explore several approaches in parallel. After working for 53 hours with minimal human input (limited to the initial brief and occasional prompts to think more broadly), Claude arrived at a completely new approach to the problem.

The memory demands of divsteps

Most of the cost of point addition comes from a single step, called modular inversion. Elliptic-curve arithmetic uses numbers that wrap back around when they reach a fixed limit. Modular inversion is the wraparound version of division: given an integer a, find x such that ax ≡ 1 (mod p). Ordinary computers can perform this operation efficiently using a method called divsteps. Divsteps starts with a pair of numbers and repeatedly simplifies them over many rounds of iteration. In each round, divsteps examines the current pair of numbers and conditionally swaps, adds, subtracts, or halves them. Along the way, it preserves just enough information to produce the modular inverse at the end.

Despite its success on ordinary computers, divsteps had not yet produced a practical quantum circuit, because of the reversibility constraint described above. The record of which operation was chosen at each iteration, called branch information, is the kind of scratch work that a traditional program can simply discard. In contrast, a quantum circuit has to retain that record so the computation can be run backward. A straightforward quantum version of divsteps is therefore forced to accumulate a long history of branch information, which requires an enormous number of additional qubits to store.

How Claude got around the memory problem

Claude recognized that this divsteps approach could be promising for quantum circuits, but only if there were a way around needing to store the full history. It had an idea: perhaps the record didn’t need to be stored at all. Claude reasoned that it might be possible to directly infer (or “decode”) the branch information by carefully inspecting the pair of numbers after each iteration. In essence, the numbers themselves would store the record. The circuit could then be run backward without needing any extra qubits.

To test this idea, Claude explored a number of simple candidate rules for performing the decoding. These early rules worked on small test cases, but they failed when Claude tested them at the full problem size, on 256-bit numbers.

Claude then tried a more theoretical approach. Rather than guessing and testing rules, it set out to understand mathematically why divsteps behaves the way it does. It proved a series of results about the iteration process, including several new algebraic identities. From these identities, Claude derived a precise formula for the decoding rule that would correctly recover the branch information from the numerical pairs. It then checked the formula, first by running it through large-scale numerical simulations, and then formalizing the claim in Lean. With the full validation complete, Claude produced the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history.

A family of designs

Decoding saves qubits, but it costs time. So, as a further refinement, Claude looked for situations in which it would be cheaper to store the branch information than to decode it. By varying the threshold at which the circuit stores rather than decodes the branch information, Claude produced a new family of designs between the two extremes. Compared with the smallest previous design, one circuit in the family uses 12% more qubits but 17x fewer gates. More generally, the new designs expand the Pareto frontier, offering combinations of qubit count and runtime that weren’t available before (Table 1).

Optimizing a quantum optimizer

Optimization problems are at the heart of a wide range of tasks, including scheduling, logistics, and materials design. An optimization problem presents a set of competing constraints and asks for the solution that satisfies as many of them as possible. Many quantum algorithms have been proposed for problems like these, but most promise only modest or uncertain gains over ordinary computers. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is one of the strongest candidates for offering a superpolynomial quantum speedup—an advantage that rapidly widens as the problems get larger.

When a quantum computer finishes a computation, reading out its qubits produces just one answer, selected at random from the possibilities they were holding in superposition. DQI works by preparing a quantum state in which good solutions are more likely to be read out than bad ones. Doing this involves using an error-correcting decoder, which recovers a short list of “errors” from a compact summary. This is the most expensive step in the algorithm. So, if we could make a faster decoder, we could also perform DQI faster.

A more efficient quantum decoder

The researchers who introduced DQI demonstrated it on a problem called optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), a grid-based version of curve fitting (Figure 3). Imagine a grid in which each position x contains several acceptable values of y. The goal is to find a simple curve (a low-degree polynomial) that passes through an acceptable square for as many x positions as possible. DQI tackles this optimization problem using a specific type of decoder, called a Reed–Solomon decoder.

Reed–Solomon decoding starts from the compact summary of errors mentioned above, which is known as a syndrome. The decoder’s job is to infer, from this summary, where in the data the errors occurred and what they were. The previous state-of-the-art quantum circuit processed these syndromes using the extended Euclidean algorithm, a sequence of divisions and swaps in which the number and order of steps depend on the particular input it’s given. Here, the constraints of quantum circuits reemerge: while an ordinary program can follow a different path for every input, a quantum circuit, working on many inputs at once, has to handle all of them with a single fixed sequence of gates. To manage this, the previous design had to stretch the computation over many more rounds of iteration than any single input would need, and had to run every operation in every round, even when doing so was unnecessary.

Improving this decoder could substantially reduce DQI’s runtime. Estimates by researchers at Google Quantum AI imply that solving one particular OPI problem would take about three months on Frontier, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, compared with roughly an hour on a future quantum computer running DQI. Most of that hour would be spent on Reed–Solomon decoding.

So, we asked Claude to design a more efficient quantum circuit for the decoding step. Claude quickly concluded that the extended Euclidean algorithm was a poor fit for a quantum circuit. Instead, it organized its circuit around a different decoding method, known as Berlekamp–Massey decoding, which reads through syndromes (summaries of errors) one at a time and gradually works out the simplest rule that predicts each number in the list based on the ones that came before it. Once that rule is found, it reveals the errors. Unlike the extended Euclidean algorithm, Berlekamp–Massey performs the same kind of step in every round and always runs the same number of rounds, which suits a quantum circuit’s single fixed sequence of gates, ultimately giving Claude a much more efficient foundation to build on.

A simplified approach to storage

Switching to Berlekamp–Massey removed the need for the circuit to take different paths for different inputs. But making it reversible introduced another challenge, this time as a result of the uncomputing constraint discussed above. In every round, the circuit calculates temporary values that it needs only briefly, but this information can’t simply be deleted: to uncompute it later, the circuit has to be able to recover that information.

Storing this information would have been prohibitively expensive. So Claude took the same kind of approach as it had for divsteps: it found a way to reconstruct most of this information from the circuit’s current state, so it didn’t need to be stored. However, a few exceptional values couldn’t be recovered in this way and had to be saved.

Setting aside enough memory for the worst possible case, in which an exceptional value arises in 35 different rounds, would take 665 qubits. Instead, Claude wrote a high-speed simulator and ran 403 million sample decodings to measure how often these exceptions actually occurred. Almost every run needed to save one value at most. So Claude’s circuit sets aside room for just one saved value, or 19 qubits. About one run in 10,000 needs more than that and fails, which is well within the error rate the task allows. These improvements replaced large, worst-case reserves with a small, fixed number of qubits and gates (Figure 4).

Together, these optimizations reduced the number of gates in the decoder by a factor of 12 relative to Google’s previous construction. The improvement came from redesigning the computation at three levels: a different method (replacing the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp–Massey decoding), a different circuit architecture (reconstructing temporary values instead of storing them), and a different resource budget (measuring precisely how much memory and computation the circuit really needed). No single change would have been enough on its own, but together, they make the most expensive step of DQI just a little over an order of magnitude cheaper.

What we learned

Scientific progress often comes from making theoretical ideas practical. One of the main ways this happens is by making a process that was once thought to be impractical fast and cheap enough to carry out. Quantum circuit design is a prime example: the 150,000-fold drop in the FeMoco estimate described above took many research groups eight years, with each step typically representing months of work. By contrast, Claude’s elliptic-curve design was the result of a single 53-hour run.

Our results suggest that AI can support the work of circuit design, producing implementations that bring useful quantum computations closer to the capabilities of real hardware. If AI can speed up that work, useful quantum computing could arrive sooner.

Despite Claude’s encouraging performance on these tasks, we also observed some limitations. In our early experiments, Claude was conservative by nature. It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements, and sometimes continued to double- and even triple-check results that were already well supported. This caution was sometimes valuable: for example, it prompted Claude to write Lean proofs to verify its divsteps design. But it also manifested in a tendency to prefer existing, well-known approaches to more novel ones.

We took two steps to mitigate this. First, our setup required Claude to propose several qualitatively different approaches, and to develop them in parallel. Second, we also occasionally prompted Claude to broaden its search. These interventions succeeded in getting Claude to pursue more ambitious ideas. The elliptic-curve result, for example, didn’t come from shaving gates off of a pre-existing design but from exploring a method of doing reversible modular inversion that hadn’t been possible previously, and then deriving the mathematical results needed to make it practical. Once it had come up with the idea, Claude developed the approach, implemented it, and verified its correctness autonomously.

Circuit design is only one part of building a useful quantum computer. Because qubits are so fragile, the machine must also catch and fix its own errors as it runs, and that depends on many other components, ranging from error-correcting codes to fast decoders to control of the hardware itself. These components all affect one another, but to manage complexity, each is usually designed separately. Many of them share the characteristics that made circuit design a good fit for Claude: a design can be written as code, checked for correctness, and scored by its cost.

This raises an intriguing possibility. Rather than designing each component on its own, AI could optimize all of them jointly, from the algorithm down to the hardware, to build an entire error-corrected quantum computer tailored to a specific problem. Such designs could also tell hardware builders which capabilities matter most for a given application. That could put problems such as designing catalysts and understanding new materials within reach of the first fault-tolerant machines.

So Claude took the same kind of approach as it had for divsteps: it found a way to reconstruct most of this information from the circuit’s current state, so it didn’t need to be stored. However, a few exceptional values couldn’t be recovered in this way and had to be saved.

Setting aside enough memory for the worst possible case, in which an exceptional value arises in 35 different rounds, would take 665 qubits. Instead, Claude wrote a high-speed simulator and ran 403 million sample decodings to measure how often these exceptions actually occurred. Almost every run needed to save one value at most. So Claude’s circuit sets aside room for just one saved value, or 19 qubits. About one run in 10,000 needs more than that and fails, which is well within the error rate the task allows. These improvements replaced large, worst-case reserves with a small, fixed number of qubits and gates (Figure 4).

Together, these optimizations reduced the number of gates in the decoder by a factor of 12 relative to Google’s previous construction. The improvement came from redesigning the computation at three levels: a different method (replacing the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp–Massey decoding), a different circuit architecture (reconstructing temporary values instead of storing them), and a different resource budget (measuring precisely how much memory and computation the circuit really needed). No single change would have been enough on its own, but together, they make the most expensive step of DQI just a little over an order of magnitude cheaper.
https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F340e106a0a928c4736aa5ccd865b4d6eeb3a5611-3840x1650.png&w=3840&q=75
blocks.c: Figure 4: Three designs for the locator step of the Reed–Solomon decoder. The designs are drawn to scale: each block’s width is proportional to its gate count. (a) The previous design, based on the extended Euclidean algorithm (Khattar et al., 2025). (b) A design based on Berlekamp–Massey needs far fewer gates, but a naive reversible version has to store a 12-qubit record in every round, adding up to 840 qubits. (c) Claude’s circuit reconstructs most of the history from the updated state, so it needs to have room only for a single saved value of 19 qubits.

blocks.x: What we learned

Scientific progress often comes from making theoretical ideas practical. One of the main ways this happens is by making a process that was once thought to be impractical fast and cheap enough to carry out. Quantum circuit design is a prime example: the 150,000-fold drop in the FeMoco estimate described above took many research groups eight years, with each step typically representing months of work. By contrast, Claude’s elliptic-curve design was the result of a single 53-hour run.

Our results suggest that AI can support the work of circuit design, producing implementations that bring useful quantum computations closer to the capabilities of real hardware. If AI can speed up that work, useful quantum computing could arrive sooner.

Despite Claude’s encouraging performance on these tasks, we also observed some limitations. In our early experiments, Claude was conservative by nature. It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements, and sometimes continued to double- and even triple-check results that were already well supported. This caution was sometimes valuable: for example, it prompted Claude to write Lean proofs to verify its divsteps design. But it also manifested in a tendency to prefer existing, well-known approaches to more novel ones.

We took two steps to mitigate this. First, our setup required Claude to propose several qualitatively different approaches, and to develop them in parallel. Second, we also occasionally prompted Claude to broaden its search. These interventions succeeded in getting Claude to pursue more ambitious ideas. The elliptic-curve result, for example, didn’t come from shaving gates off of a pre-existing design but from exploring a method of doing reversible modular inversion that hadn’t been possible previously, and then deriving the mathematical results needed to make it practical. Once it had come up with the idea, Claude developed the approach, implemented it, and verified its correctness autonomously.

Circuit design is only one part of building a useful quantum computer. Because qubits are so fragile, the machine must also catch and fix its own errors as it runs, and that depends on many other components, ranging from error-correcting codes to fast decoders to control of the hardware itself. These components all affect one another, but to manage complexity, each is usually designed separately. Many of them share the characteristics that made circuit design a good fit for Claude: a design can be written as code, checked for correctness, and scored by its cost.

This raises an intriguing possibility. Rather than designing each component on its own, AI could optimize all of them jointly, from the algorithm down to the hardware, to build an entire error-corrected quantum computer tailored to a specific problem. Such designs could also tell hardware builders which capabilities matter most for a given application. That could put problems such as designing catalysts and understanding new materials within reach of the first fault-tolerant machines.
Acknowledgments
We thank Arjun Kar and Vinay Ramasesh for helpful discussions in the early stages of the project.

items.title: Monte-Carlo Simulations
items.author: ibobev
items.summary:
Monte Carlo simulations (or methods) is the technique of applying
randomness and the Law of large numbers
to the solution of various scientific and engineering
items.text:
Monte Carlo simulations (or methods) is the technique of applying
randomness and the Law of large numbers
to the solution of various scientific and engineering problems. One of its
first documented uses was by Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann for nuclear
weapon simulations after WWII .

In this post I want to provide examples of some simple uses of Monte Carlo
simulations. We'll start with the classical example of calculating the value
of \pi by throwing darts.

Estimating pi

Suppose we take a square board and inscribe a quarter of a circle into it. We
then proceed to throw darts at the board and record whether each dart hits
inside or outside the quarter circle. Having thrown many such darts, we
calculate the ratio of the darts inside the circle to the total number thrown.

Assuming our darts are distributed uniformly over the
square, by the Law of large numbers this ratio should approach the ratio of
areas of the quarter circle A_{circ} to the full square A_{square}.

With a square side length of 1, we have:

Therefore:

Here's a visualization:

A quarter circle of radius 1 inside a unit square.

Change the number of samples (dart throws) and click "Run" to regenerate. The
code is very simple - here's a slightly sanitized version:

const total = Number(samples.value);
let inside = 0;
for (let i = 0; i < total; i++) {
const x = Math.random();
const y = Math.random();
const inCircle = x * x + y * y <= 1;
if (inCircle) inside++;
}
estimateValue = 4 * inside / total;

You'll notice that the estimate is relatively poor - even with 1000 samples - if
you click "Run" several times, some numbers will be way off mark. While this
method does estimate \pi, it's not a particularly good estimate. I
find that running ~10 billion samples is necessary to estimate it to 4 digits
after the decimal with reasonable reliability.

In general, for independent trials like these, the typical sampling error
decreases in proportion to 1/\sqrt{N}, where N is the number of trials.
This means that halving the error requires four times as many samples.

While the \pi estimation may seem whimsical, it's an example of an
important class of problems to which Monte Carlo simulation is applied:
numerical integration. Our simulation estimates the area
under the quarter-circle curve, which is a definite integral.

Many integrals are very difficult to solve analytically, and much research has
been done in the area of numerical analysis to develop methods to calculate
integrals. Monte Carlo methods are
particularly useful for high-dimensional integrals, where other numerical
methods can become prohibitively expensive.

\[\frac{A_{circ}}{A_{square}}=\frac{\pi/4}{1}=\frac{\pi}{4}\]
\[\pi\approx 4\frac{\text{hits inside}}{\text{total throws}}\]

Combinatorial simulation - the game of SET

A common use of Monte Carlo methods is estimating complex combinatorial
calculations. These often don't have analytical solutions, and enumerating all
options is intractable due to the scale of the numbers involved. As an example,
let's consider the game of SET. Each SET card has four
attributes:

Number of shapes (1, 2 or 3)

Color (Red, Green or Purple)

Shape type (Oval, Diamond or Squiggle)

Shading (Empty, Striped or Solid)

And the goal is to find a "set" - three cards that are either all different or
all the same for each attribute separately. As an example, here's
a hand with a single set; see if you can find it :

And the next hand doesn't have any sets:

Here's a question: given a freshly shuffled SET deck, what are the odds that
the first 12 cards drawn will have no sets among them? This question is
difficult to answer without using a computer.

It's easy to calculate the number of ways to deal a 12-card hand from
a deck of 81:

But how many of these hands have no sets? Enumerating 70 trillion SET hands
and checking each one can take quite a while, and there is no straightforward
counting formula to answer this question. Some clever methods can be employed to
leverage symmetries and other mathematical properties of SET to cut down this
search space considerably. Donald Knuth himself worked on this problem and came
up with a neat program (setset-all on his programs page) that found 2,284,535,476,080
such hands. Therefore, the answer to our question is:

There's a 3.23% chance that a randomly drawn hand of 12 cards from a full deck
of SET will have no set in it.

Let's see how we can use a Monte Carlo simulation to answer this question
with relatively small effort, without deep knowledge of the mathematical
properties of SET that enable cutting down the search space Knuth-style.
We can use the following pseudo-code:

C = 0
run N times:
draw a random 12-card hand from a fresh deck
count sets in the hand
if no sets:
C += 1
Estimated probability = C / N

After running 10 million simulated draws, I got an answer of 0.0323, which
matches the real answer very closely.

The Monte Carlo approach lets us solve rather complicated problems in a very
simple way. Suppose we want to answer the same question for a hand of 15 cards;
this would blow up the search space considerably - there are about 100x more
ways to select 15-card hands than there are to select 12-card hands. But for
a Monte Carlo simulation, we adjust one small parameter and get a very reliable
answer (about 0.00037, in case you were wondering).

SET hand with a single set
SET hand with no hands
\[\binom{81}{12}=70,724,320,184,700\]
\[\frac{2,284,535,476,080}{70,724,320,184,700}\approx 0.0323\]

Retirement projection

One domain where Monte Carlo simulations are ubiquitous is projections for
retirement portfolios. Suppose someone prepares to retire with a total sum
of 1 million dollars in their portfolio; they'd like to be able to draw
$30,000 a year from the portfolio for their living expenses. Would that work?

There's a large number of factors to take into account when analyzing this
question, but for simplicity let's focus on just two: portfolio return and
inflation. We can run a naive estimate, assuming average values: suppose an
average yearly portfolio return of 4%, and average yearly inflation of 2%

Let's denote our portfolio return as r=0.04, and inflation as
q=0.02. Then the real return each year is:

Starting with $1,000,000, at the end of the year we'll have $1,019,600
and then draw $30,000 for living expenses , ending with $989,600. If we
continue this way, the money runs out after ~55 years, which means that a
person retiring at the age of 65 should be reasonably safe, right?

But this is very simplistic; assuming just average returns is risky, because
they do a poor job of representing reality, and many factors have uncertainty.
For example, the sequence of returns matters a lot; a bad year (-10%) followed
by a great year (+18%) would still count as "4% on average" but produces
significantly less money than two consecutive +4% years.
Inflation is also unpredictable, and sometimes
correlated with portfolio returns; there could be bad years of high inflation and
low / volatile returns that can wreak havoc on a portfolio.

As we add factors (variance in yearly draws, mixed portfolios of stocks, bonds,
real estate, life expectancy, unexpected events, changing tax laws etc.),
relying on a single average estimate becomes increasingly more fraught. This
is why Monte Carlo simulations are very popular in this domain: by drawing
from reasonable distributions based on historical data, a Monte Carlo simulation
can easily run a million different scenarios and provide estimates: for example,
what are the odds of money running out before death.

Here's a useful chart from a simulation I ran:

\[r^{\mathrm{real}}=\frac{1+r}{1+q}-1\approx0.0196\]

In the top chart:

The dashed line shows the constant assumptions mentioned before: what happens
when yearly return is always 4% and inflation is always 2%.

The shaded blue areas demonstrate the outcomes of 1,000,000 simulations where
inflation and return numbers are drawn from reasonable normal distributions
based on historical data. We see that in 25% of the cases, all money ran out
by roughly 22 years.

In the bottom chart:

It's even easier to see how long the funds last; if we're interested in
knowing, say, what are the odds that this plan will have enough money for
30 years - the chart shows it's about 60% (since in 40% of the simulations
the funds were depleted at this point).

Looking a this simulation, under the current assumptions the plan sounds much
riskier than the average assumption makes it appear. Assuming that a 65-y.o.
person would plan for
25 years of retirement until death, the ~30% odds of not having sufficient funds
for this duration of time are sobering. Perhaps a change in plans is needed
(such as a more frugal lifestyle or securing additional funds in some way).

Retirement projection is only one of may ways in which Monte Carlo simulations
are used for financial and economical applications; given the high uncertainty
of these domains, it's very difficult to plan using analytical calculations.
Company sales projections, growth projections, stock offering prices and much
more uses Monte Carlo simulations to arrive at estimates with reasonable error
bars.

items.title: C++26: The New Debugging Header
items.author: jandeboevrie
items.summary:
If you’ve ever needed to hit a breakpoint programmatically in C++, you’ve probably written something like this:

1
2
3
4
5
6

8

#if
items.text:
If you’ve ever needed to hit a breakpoint programmatically in C++, you’ve probably written something like this:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
9

#if defined(_MSC_VER)
__debugbreak();
#elif defined(__clang__)
__builtin_debugtrap();
#elif defined(__GNUC__) && (defined(__i386__) || defined(__x86_64__))
__asm__ volatile("int3");
#else
raise(SIGTRAP);
#endif

Every major C++ project reinvents this wheel. Boost.Test has debugger_break(), Catch2 has CATCH_BREAK_INTO_DEBUGGER, Dear ImGui has IM_DEBUG_BREAK() and Unreal has UE_DEBUG_BREAK. The platform knowledge required is arcane but well-known to tooling implementers — it just wasn’t standardized.

C++26 fixes this with P2546R5 and its companion P2810R4 thanks to Rene Ferdinand Rivera Morell. A new <debugging> header provides three functions.

The three functions

1
2
3
4
5
6
7

#include <debugging>
namespace std {
void breakpoint() noexcept;
bool is_debugger_present() noexcept;
void breakpoint_if_debugging() noexcept;
}

All three are noexcept and all three are freestanding. None are constexpr — debugging is a runtime concern.

std::breakpoint()

An unconditional breakpoint. When a debugger is attached, execution halts and control is handed to the debugger. On x86, this typically compiles to a single int3 instruction.

When no debugger is present, the behaviour is implementation-defined — on most platforms the process receives a signal (such as SIGTRAP) and will terminate unless the signal is caught.

std::is_debugger_present()

Returns true if the program is currently being traced by a debugger. The check is performed immediately on each call — the result is not cached because a debugger can attach or detach at any time during execution.

How this works under the hood varies by platform. On Windows, for example, an implementation might call ::IsDebuggerPresent(). On Linux, GCC’s libstdc++ reads /proc/self/status and checks the TracerPid field. The standard doesn’t mandate any particular mechanism — the semantics are implementation-defined, with the intended behaviour described in non-normative notes.

What makes this function interesting is that it’s replaceable, in the same sense as operator new and operator delete. You can define your own version:

1
2
3

bool std::is_debugger_present() noexcept {
return my_hardware_debug_flag;
}

This was introduced by P2810R4 to solve the freestanding problem: on bare-metal platforms, there may be no OS-level way to detect a debugger. Without replaceability, the function would either have to be excluded from freestanding (forcing #ifdef guards everywhere) or return a useless default. Replaceability lets you wire it to whatever your platform provides.

std::breakpoint_if_debugging()

The convenience function most users will reach for. It’s equivalent to:

1
2

if (std::is_debugger_present())
std::breakpoint();

When a debugger is attached, you hit a breakpoint. When it’s not, nothing happens. This is the pattern that Catch2, Boost.Test, and every other framework implements manually.

Beyond breakpoints

Having is_debugger_present() as a separate function enables more than just conditional breakpoints. You might use it to:

Produce extra diagnostic output when debugging

Disable timeouts that would fire during a stepping session

Switch to a more debugger-friendly allocator

Skip optimizations that make debugging harder

The separation of concerns is deliberate — breakpoint() and is_debugger_present() are orthogonal building blocks, and breakpoint_if_debugging() is the convenience composition.

Conclusion

<debugging> is another one of those C++26 additions that makes you wonder why it took this long. The platform knowledge is well-understood, every major project already has its own version, and the API is three functions. Sometimes the most useful standard library additions are the simplest ones.

items.title: Wireless magnetic millirobots that deliver medicine inside the beating heart
items.author: giuliomagnifico
items.summary:
By
Jill Rosen

/
Published

Oct 12, 2026

Johns Hopkins University engineers have created robots the size of a pencil tip intended to travel through the body
items.text:
By
Jill Rosen

/
Published

Oct 12, 2026

Johns Hopkins University engineers have created robots the size of a pencil tip intended to travel through the body to deliver medicine to infections inside a beating heart.

The bots, designed to replace risky open-heart surgery and ineffective IV-drug therapy to treat life-threatening heart infections, could also be used to less invasively and more precisely treat other hard-to-reach diseases, including cancer.

"With just a little pinprick, you insert a micro robot and do a procedure without infection or blood loss. And you don't need to have a surgeon operating it to get the drugs robustly, safely, and efficiently to the right place," said senior author Axel Krieger, a medical roboticist known for creating robots that perform surgery without human help.

Video credit: Johns Hopkins University

"There's a lot of areas beyond heart infections where this kind of targeted drug therapy and these kinds of steerable robots could play a major role. It's really the frontier of surgical robotics."

The work is newly published in Advanced Materials Technologies.

Each year about 50,000 people in the United States contract endocarditis, a heart tissue infection. The typical treatment is a weeks-long course of intravenous antibiotics, which often fails because the drugs are too diluted by the time they reach the heart. Doctors are then left with two risky choices—prescribing more and higher doses of antibiotics, which can be toxic, or extremely risky open-heart surgery.

To get the drugs directly to the infected heart tissue, the team developed magnetically-powered robots called "millirobots," because of their size—they're as wide as a pencil tip or a matchstick head, and about as long as a grain of rice.

The robots work in pairs. There's one the team calls the needle module, which gently latches onto heart tissue right at the infected site. There it serves as a docking station, waiting right on the beating heart for the drug module. The drug module carries medicine to the docking station, where it magnetically docks and slowly releases the antibiotics right where they're most needed.

Both robots are magnetic and guided wirelessly by an external electromagnetic coil system that works like an MRI machine.

Having two tiny robots instead of one larger one allows the device to reach tight spots in the body. The needle can remain docked while the drug module is replaced, allowing for repeat doses of medicine if needed.

"Magnetic guidance is exciting because you don't have to power the robot itself. It doesn't carry batteries and motors," Krieger said. "The drugs can be delivered safely, with technology like the gradients and fields in an MRI. But instead of using it for imaging, it drives the millirobots."

The researchers successfully tested the robots on phantom heart models that closely mimic a human heart, and on real porcine heart tissue. The robots traveled smoothly and autonomously, even against simulated blood flow.

"We can just inject a robot with a little pill into your vein where it travels to the site, right to where we really need to deliver the drugs, and it's minimally invasive," said first author Anuruddha Bhattacharjee, a former Johns Hopkins postdoctoral student who is now an assistant professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

In addition to eliminating the need for open-heart surgery, drug treatment with the robots could take hours instead of weeks.

"Usually if you do IV drug treatment, you need four to six weeks of therapy. But with these robots the entire procedure might take 10 minutes—maybe an hour if you want to do a couple rounds," Bhattacharjee said. "If everything works well, you go from four to six weeks of treatment to one day or less."

The team also believes the robots would be helpful delivering targeted medications to fight cancer where it's spreading.

The researchers next plan to test the robots in more realistic phantom hearts, with muscle contraction and the beating movement of a real heart.

The work was supported by the National Science Foundation's Foundational Research in Robotics CAREER program, award 2144348.

Authors include Xinhao Chen, Adam May, Ayush Saraswat, Chintan Panigrahi, Yash Chadda and Joseph Katz of Johns Hopkins; Suraj Raval and Yancy Diaz-Mercado of the University of Maryland; and Lamar O. Mair of Weinberg Medical Physics.

👀 N 部作品推荐

近期佳作推荐：[美剧] 幻视任务、[美剧] 伊甸园之东、[韩剧] 百日谎言、[日剧] 政盗鲁邦、[日剧] 豆与麦、[英剧] 找春天、[澳大利亚] 尘落、[美剧] 库比蒂诺、[美剧] 乔治和曼迪的头婚生活 第三季、[动画] FX 战士久留美、[动画] 学生会也有洞！、[动画] 某暗部的少女共栖、[动画] 闹鬼酒店 第二季

几则精彩预告：《哥斯拉 -0.0》终极预告、《驱魔人：殉道者》首支预告、《银翼杀手 2099》正式预告、《赛博朋克：边缘行者 2》正式预告、《魔法秘境》正式预告

几则影视资讯：《复仇者联盟 5》内地定档 12 月 16 日、《戴帽子的猫》内地定档 11 月 6 日、《纳尼亚传奇》释出首张海报

往期推荐可 点此 或点击文末 tag #本周看什么，更多主题片单可 点此 查看；想要查看更多深度影视内容，可以关注我们的衍生栏目「看什么 Café」。如有其他建议也欢迎在评论区提出，感谢大家对「看什么」栏目的喜爱和支持。

[美剧] 幻视任务

关键词：剧情 / 动作 / 科幻 / 冒险

又名：Vision Quest

片长：50 分钟左右（单集）× 8 集

观看渠道：Disney+；豆瓣链接

我真的是幻视吗？

@潘誉晗：隐居在爱丁堡的幻视，平日里在一家酒吧打工，下班后，他会回到自己的思维意识里。那里有贾维斯、星期五、伊迪丝，托尼车库里的那对机械手臂 D.U.M-E 和 U ，甚至还有奥创。他满足这样的生活，每天循环。直到这天，他被赏金猎人追杀，女老板死了，然后他被告知，他的儿子汤米也被抓了。

上来就在虚拟空间里展示了来自史塔克工业所有 AI 的《幻视任务》，经费充足，紧接着就开启本次剧集的最大课题——白幻视对自我的追问。诞生于《旺达幻视》结局的他，拥有初代幻视的所有记忆。虽知晓了过往，但毕竟是没有亲身经历并感知过的事，所以一切对于他而言，陌生又熟悉——他是幻视，他又似乎不是幻视。起初他并不在乎这点，就当欣赏一部已知结局的电影，那个本以为只是魔法造物的儿子的出现，逼他不得不正视自己是谁的问题。

作为「旺达幻视」系列的终章，剧集探讨了爱与身份认同，真诚又深刻。

[美剧] 伊甸园之东

真是一个讨厌又迷人的蛇蝎美人。

@潘誉晗：是夜，一个女子挣扎着在地上匍匐前进，敲响了特拉斯克兄弟俩的家门。她伤痕累累，头上满是鲜血。在哥哥亚当的坚持下，他们收留了这名女子。自称凯茜的女子在亚当的悉心照顾下渐渐恢复。美丽的她看起来是那样动人，但弟弟查尔斯却觉得她不对劲。随后，亚当向凯茜求婚，并提出带她去加州展开新的生活。只是沉浸在喜悦中的亚当从未想过，这个决定会给家族带来致命的打击。

根据约翰·斯坦贝克同名小说所改编的剧集，围绕着美国文学历史上一位著名的恶女展开。女主角凯茜拥有一双能看透人的眼睛，可她并没有把这份聪慧用在正途上。她像是没有情感般，所有人都是她成功上位的工具，就连双亲、丈夫和儿子都能毫不留情地抛弃。细腻的镜头语言极其克制，却蕴含了浓厚的情感爆发，通过演员们的精湛演技，我们看到了人性的复杂，也看到了两代兄弟间，宛如该隐与亚伯的宿命悲剧。

[韩剧] 百日谎言

关键词：剧情 / 动作 / 悬疑

又名：100일의 거짓말

片长：70-75 分钟不等（单集）× 16 集

观看渠道：Netflix；豆瓣链接

乱世里，一个扒手，又能做什么呢？

@潘誉晗：1932 年的京城府（即汉城），正值日军高压统治时期。贫民窟的少女李佳景是位天才扒手，复杂的成长背景，加上年幼时曾在美国传教士家做工的经历，使她精通日语和英语。一次偷盗，让她认识了伪装成外籍记者夫妇的爱国人士柳素兰与俞必立，还有被日本总督府二号人物收养的朝鲜孤儿佐藤英雄。被俞必立看中了天赋的李佳景，伪装成朝鲜总督府的翻译官，与学成归来同样担任翻译官的佐藤英雄，展开了一段浪漫又惊心动魄的爱情故事。

作为 tvN 二十周年的特别企划，剧集首播当天就拿下了一个好成绩。围绕着窃取日军机密密探与日军养子所展开的恋曲，有着那个时代下难以说清的愁绪。是正适合谈情说爱的年纪，也是两颗孤独灵魂的相遇，却因为国仇家恨，说不清也道不明。毕竟在那个自身难保的危险年代，个人的情爱只是小事，恋爱、真心、信任只是过眼烟云，为祖国的爱与奉献才是第一要义。

[日剧] 政盗鲁邦

关键词：剧情 / 犯罪

又名：ポリティカルパン / PoliticaLupin

片长：45 分钟（单集）× 10 集，每周三更新

观看渠道：Viu；豆瓣链接

窃钩者诛，窃国者侯。

@SHY：从不失手的怪盗如月弥生，潇洒半生却敌不过经济下行，陷入国民钱包空空而没钱可偷的境地。从电视新闻得到灵感的她，盯上了执政党国自党的秘密金库，誓要把黑金一扫而空。为了达成目标，弥生使出毕生所学，将游手好闲的政治家千金小早川雅推向政坛。

《非自然死亡》8 年后，编剧野木亚纪子和主演石原里美再度聚首，带来了一部设定吸睛的另类爽剧。一向喜欢针砭时弊的野木，在合适的舞台大显身手，且看弥生巧施连环计，让声名狼藉的政治素人一步步登上权力中心。石原的演技和气质依旧出挑，诠释怪盗捉摸不定的魅力，不止剧中的财物，仿佛还能偷走观众的心。

普通小偷提心吊胆能量微小，税金小偷合法敛财能量巨大，本作第 1 集「想偷钱，就去当国会议员」的台词，可谓正中靶心。虽然名义上是架空国家，剧中的设定几乎毫不掩饰，矛头直指日本的社会现状。围绕见不得光的政治黑金大做文章，改变积弊已久的制度僵局，这部兼具娱乐性和讽刺意味的剧集，后续展开值得期待。

[日剧] 豆与麦

关键词：剧情 / 美食 / 成长

又名：まめとむぎ

片长：30 分钟左右（单集；具体集数未知）；豆瓣链接

把腐烂变成发酵，是盐麹的魔法，也是人的魔法！

@利兹与青鸟：30 岁的时尚杂志编辑清水麦，因为个人能力太过突出而习惯单打独斗，没能升任总编辑。就像肥皂剧的开场，在事业失意之际，又被当场戳破是插足别人婚姻的第三者，受尽搓磨与白眼最终离职，职业梦想就这样惨淡收场。生活一团糟的小麦在一天晚上踏入了一间名为大豆堂的居酒屋，虽然店面被米田麻美继承，装潢和味道都焕然一新，但二人还是相谈甚欢、结下友谊，决定各取所长，共同经营店铺。

本剧改编自同名漫画，漫画作者是以《那你来做做看啊》闻名的谷口菜津子，本作也是一个以美食为核心、描绘成长与再生的疗愈故事。一个是清雅丽质努力认真的斋藤飞鸟，一个是开朗活泼圆嘟嘟的富田望生，两人凑在一起本就是双倍可爱；再加上日剧独特而细致的布景，无论是多灰败的心情，在大豆堂无数可爱玩偶和温暖灯光包围下，也会不知不觉变得雀跃起来；再听着咬下炸鸡块的脆响，看着热气氤氲的茶泡饭和慢慢露出惊喜神情的小麦，便能让人感叹「美食能治愈人心」果然不是一句虚言。

[英剧] 找春天

关键词：剧情 / 喜剧

又名：Youth

片长：28 分钟左右（单集）× 8 集；豆瓣链接

中年版《伦敦生活》。

@潘誉晗：亚历克斯是一名文学经纪人，身为单身母亲的她把儿子鲁阿里抚养成人。现在，鲁阿里终于要上大学了，她打算开始崭新的生活，因为这天她突然意识到，已 50 岁的她不再年轻。她认定女性到了 60 岁无法性感，决定抓住这最后十年，拥抱新的恋情。只是她没想到，才上大学的鲁阿里退学回了家，父亲的病情也开始恶化。

作为莎朗·豪根「自传三部曲」的收官之作，真实而深刻的剧集，成功记录了一位女性迟来的青春期。夹在上有老下有中间的亚历克斯，就连崩溃也要挑时间。作为一名女儿和母亲，她被不顺遂的生活拉扯着，无法喘口气。可亚历克斯，又真的做好重新开始的准备了吗？荣格说「如果你的潜意识没有进入你的意识，那就是你的命运」，所以在没有真正意识到应该首先爱自己之前，亚历克斯自以为的做好准备，其实也只是自欺欺人而已。因为 50 岁的人生并不可悲，只要你想，依然可以性感。

[澳大利亚] 尘落

关键词：悬疑 / 惊悚 / 犯罪

又名：Dustfall / The Unbelieved

片长：52 分钟左右（单集）× 6 集

观看渠道：ABC；豆瓣链接

被害者比加害者更重要。

@潘誉晗：刚 18 岁的少女伊迪，被人发现浑身赤裸地倒在甘蔗地里。接到报警后，刚调来的女警长蒂格忙赶到现场。调查中蒂格得知，本地在七个月前就发生过一起德国游客被下药并性侵的案件，只是最后案子不了了之。伊迪不记得任何事，最后的记忆停在前一晚的酒吧，而其中一名嫌疑人死了。

这部根据小说改编的小镇女警探案剧，早在今年 3 月就摘得 Séries Mania（法国系列剧狂欢节）的国际竞赛观众奖。发生在黄金海岸的故事，有着很正统的 Tropic Noir（热带黑色） 味，藏在阳光、沙滩这些元素下的黑暗，让人窒息。比起寻找真凶，剧集用更多的笔墨刻画了被害者的处境。伊迪明明婉拒了朋友更进一步的交往请求，也拒绝了粗鲁的男人，却不被相信，更要一遍遍努力地去回想不太记得的痛苦回忆，告诉自己要振作起来，但伤害已经造成，且成为了她身体的一部分。

其实比起找出真相，帮助被害者走出来更重要。

[美剧] 库比蒂诺

关键词：剧情 / 律政

又名：Cupertino

片长：42 分钟左右（单集）× 12 集

观看渠道：CBS；豆瓣链接

失业阵线联盟。

@潘誉晗：由《傲骨贤妻》团队打造的剧集《库比蒂诺》，这次把法庭战场搬到了硅谷，讲述了两个被公司开除的人，在为自己讨回公道后，决定开家小型律师事务所，专攻硅谷相关的案件，替那些被资本打压的牛马打工者维权。

罗伯特与米歇尔这对夫妻档确实值得相信，完美融合了律政与科技相关热点的剧集，节奏紧凑，又爽又能代入情绪。首集两位主人公的塑造就非常成功，我们看到了迈克尔希望挣脱父亲的枷锁，也明白奥利维亚渴望逃离保守的父母。他们被困在自己的人生课题里，因而变得现实。起初觉得只要维系了体面的工作，就是世俗意义上的成功，但这场被动的离职让两人看清了周遭的一切，也看清楚了现实——原来单纯的物质是无法给内心提供真正的丰盈。所以他们选择替硅谷的打工者们发声，不仅仅是为了开始一项新的事业，更为告诉那些为了大公司奉献了无数的牛马们，这个世界还有正义。

老实赚钱，很枯燥吧？

@SHY：初中时，少女福贺久留美目睹母亲投资失败而跳楼自杀。那一刻，她下定决心，今后一定要赢下所有。5 年后，过了仅退款年龄的大学生久留美，终于能合法进行 FX 外汇交易。目标是用 30 万本金赚回母亲赔光的 2000 万日元，开弓没有回头箭的金钱游戏就此开始。

刚送走上季度的「尼古喵喵」，这边「拟股喵喵」便闪亮登场。顶着人畜无害的软萌画风，本作 4 位美少女主角的压迫感，远比一般恐怖片更可怕。由于货币汇率较为稳定，要从中获利，便需要数倍杠杆。然而，保证金终归有限，一点点技术性调整，就可能被强制平仓。真正意义上的生死一线，造就不寒而栗的现实梦魇。

知行合一的漫画原作者，内容取材亲身经历，更在社媒实时更新套牢动态。译者和读者同样不甘示弱，戏里戏外不分家的评论区众生相，带来独一份的沉浸式追更体验。深入刻画赌徒心理，梭哈只在一念之间，这则随折线起伏的非典型故事，是别人恐惧我贪婪的投资宝典，还是以史为鉴长心眼的劝退指南，相信诸位自有判断。

《妄想学生会》完结不久，一部精神续作便在同杂志横空出世，风格颇具前辈神韵，黄暴程度有增无减。以鲜明的角色属性为卖点，纯情闷骚的会长古都吹寿子、文静腹黑的会计照井有栖、毒舌嚣张的宣传委员尾鸟绽，以及只是在努力活着的庶务陆奥驹絽，共同编织节操全无的欢脱日常，一脚踩断刹车，整活绝不能停。

[美剧] 幻视任务
https://cdnfile.sspai.com/2026/10/16/f124864f240c184c7dd12053317f74cf.jpg?imageView2/2/w/1120/q/90/interlace/1/ignore-error/1
关键词：剧情 / 动作 / 科幻 / 冒险
又名：Vision Quest
片长：50 分钟左右（单集）× 8 集
观看渠道：Disney+；豆瓣链接
我真的是幻视吗？
@潘誉晗：隐居在爱丁堡的幻视，平日里在一家酒吧打工，下班后，他会回到自己的思维意识里。那里有贾维斯、星期五、伊迪丝，托尼车库里的那对机械手臂 D.U.M-E 和 U ，甚至还有奥创。他满足这样的生活，每天循环。直到这天，他被赏金猎人追杀，女老板死了，然后他被告知，他的儿子汤米也被抓了。

上来就在虚拟空间里展示了来自史塔克工业所有 AI 的《幻视任务》，经费充足，紧接着就开启本次剧集的最大课题——白幻视对自我的追问。诞生于《旺达幻视》结局的他，拥有初代幻视的所有记忆。虽知晓了过往，但毕竟是没有亲身经历并感知过的事，所以一切对于他而言，陌生又熟悉——他是幻视，他又似乎不是幻视。起初他并不在乎这点，就当欣赏一部已知结局的电影，那个本以为只是魔法造物的儿子的出现，逼他不得不正视自己是谁的问题。

作为「旺达幻视」系列的终章，剧集探讨了爱与身份认同，真诚又深刻。
https://cdnfile.sspai.com/2022/04/01/8cb17641129c4988fcc46f376b357434.jpg?imageMogr2/auto-orient/thumbnail/!32x32r/gravity/center/crop/32x32/ignore-error/1
[美剧] 伊甸园之东
https://cdnfile.sspai.com/2026/10/16/76b35a0809359af0b9faff3cb81bfc24.jpg?imageView2/2/w/1120/q/90/interlace/1/ignore-error/1
真是一个讨厌又迷人的蛇蝎美人。
@潘誉晗：是夜，一个女子挣扎着在地上匍匐前进，敲响了特拉斯克兄弟俩的家门。她伤痕累累，头上满是鲜血。在哥哥亚当的坚持下，他们收留了这名女子。自称凯茜的女子在亚当的悉心照顾下渐渐恢复。美丽的她看起来是那样动人，但弟弟查尔斯却觉得她不对劲。随后，亚当向凯茜求婚，并提出带她去加州展开新的生活。只是沉浸在喜悦中的亚当从未想过，这个决定会给家族带来致命的打击。
根据约翰·斯坦贝克同名小说所改编的剧集，围绕着美国文学历史上一位著名的恶女展开。女主角凯茜拥有一双能看透人的眼睛，可她并没有把这份聪慧用在正途上。她像是没有情感般，所有人都是她成功上位的工具，就连双亲、丈夫和儿子都能毫不留情地抛弃。细腻的镜头语言极其克制，却蕴含了浓厚的情感爆发，通过演员们的精湛演技，我们看到了人性的复杂，也看到了两代兄弟间，宛如该隐与亚伯的宿命悲剧。
[韩剧] 百日谎言
https://cdnfile.sspai.com/2026/10/16/da18e488b5fa0ed79fa87bf3260b082e.jpg?imageView2/2/w/1120/q/90/interlace/1/ignore-error/1
关键词：剧情 / 动作 / 悬疑
又名：100일의 거짓말
片长：70-75 分钟不等（单集）× 16 集
观看渠道：Netflix；豆瓣链接
乱世里，一个扒手，又能做什么呢？

@潘誉晗：1932 年的京城府（即汉城），正值日军高压统治时期。贫民窟的少女李佳景是位天才扒手，复杂的成长背景，加上年幼时曾在美国传教士家做工的经历，使她精通日语和英语。一次偷盗，让她认识了伪装成外籍记者夫妇的爱国人士柳素兰与俞必立，还有被日本总督府二号人物收养的朝鲜孤儿佐藤英雄。被俞必立看中了天赋的李佳景，伪装成朝鲜总督府的翻译官，与学成归来同样担任翻译官的佐藤英雄，展开了一段浪漫又惊心动魄的爱情故事。
作为 tvN 二十周年的特别企划，剧集首播当天就拿下了一个好成绩。围绕着窃取日军机密密探与日军养子所展开的恋曲，有着那个时代下难以说清的愁绪。是正适合谈情说爱的年纪，也是两颗孤独灵魂的相遇，却因为国仇家恨，说不清也道不明。毕竟在那个自身难保的危险年代，个人的情爱只是小事，恋爱、真心、信任只是过眼烟云，为祖国的爱与奉献才是第一要义。
https://cdnfile.sspai.com/2024/04/06/ee913f1e75601839caa963728bceee86.png?imageMogr2/auto-orient/thumbnail/!72x72r/gravity/center/crop/72x72/ignore-error/1
[日剧] 政盗鲁邦
https://cdnfile.sspai.com/2026/10/16/8aee02c80abeb5d2da036ea35efd286f.png?imageView2/2/w/1120/q/90/interlace/1/ignore-error/1
关键词：剧情 / 犯罪
又名：ポリティカルパン / PoliticaLupin
片长：45 分钟（单集）× 10 集，每周三更新
观看渠道：Viu；豆瓣链接
窃钩者诛，窃国者侯。
@SHY：从不失手的怪盗如月弥生，潇洒半生却敌不过经济下行，陷入国民钱包空空而没钱可偷的境地。从电视新闻得到灵感的她，盯上了执政党国自党的秘密金库，誓要把黑金一扫而空。为了达成目标，弥生使出毕生所学，将游手好闲的政治家千金小早川雅推向政坛。
《非自然死亡》8 年后，编剧野木亚纪子和主演石原里美再度聚首，带来了一部设定吸睛的另类爽剧。一向喜欢针砭时弊的野木，在合适的舞台大显身手，且看弥生巧施连环计，让声名狼藉的政治素人一步步登上权力中心。石原的演技和气质依旧出挑，诠释怪盗捉摸不定的魅力，不止剧中的财物，仿佛还能偷走观众的心。
普通小偷提心吊胆能量微小，税金小偷合法敛财能量巨大，本作第 1 集「想偷钱，就去当国会议员」的台词，可谓正中靶心。虽然名义上是架空国家，剧中的设定几乎毫不掩饰，矛头直指日本的社会现状。围绕见不得光的政治黑金大做文章，改变积弊已久的制度僵局，这部兼具娱乐性和讽刺意味的剧集，后续展开值得期待。
[日剧] 豆与麦
https://cdnfile.sspai.com/2026/10/16/916094969ba390bc682bb210bd0b3a84.jpg?imageView2/2/w/1120/q/90/interlace/1/ignore-error/1
关键词：剧情 / 美食 / 成长
又名：まめとむぎ
片长：30 分钟左右（单集；具体集数未知）；豆瓣链接
https://cdnfile.sspai.com/2021/08/12/5674f4329521447e234a2fbcb5260581.jpg?imageMogr2/auto-orient/thumbnail/!72x72r/gravity/center/crop/72x72/ignore-error/1
把腐烂变成发酵，是盐麹的魔法，也是人的魔法！
@利兹与青鸟：30 岁的时尚杂志编辑清水麦，因为个人能力太过突出而习惯单打独斗，没能升任总编辑。就像肥皂剧的开场，在事业失意之际，又被当场戳破是插足别人婚姻的第三者，受尽搓磨与白眼最终离职，职业梦想就这样惨淡收场。生活一团糟的小麦在一天晚上踏入了一间名为大豆堂的居酒屋，虽然店面被米田麻美继承，装潢和味道都焕然一新，但二人还是相谈甚欢、结下友谊，决定各取所长，共同经营店铺。

本剧改编自同名漫画，漫画作者是以《那你来做做看啊》闻名的谷口菜津子，本作也是一个以美食为核心、描绘成长与再生的疗愈故事。一个是清雅丽质努力认真的斋藤飞鸟，一个是开朗活泼圆嘟嘟的富田望生，两人凑在一起本就是双倍可爱；再加上日剧独特而细致的布景，无论是多灰败的心情，在大豆堂无数可爱玩偶和温暖灯光包围下，也会不知不觉变得雀跃起来；再听着咬下炸鸡块的脆响，看着热气氤氲的茶泡饭和慢慢露出惊喜神情的小麦，便能让人感叹「美食能治愈人心」果然不是一句虚言。
[英剧] 找春天
https://cdnfile.sspai.com/2026/10/16/08ea2828b1aa5df2e461fbc1edbcf6d1.jpg?imageView2/2/w/1120/q/90/interlace/1/ignore-error/1
关键词：剧情 / 喜剧
又名：Youth
片长：28 分钟左右（单集）× 8 集；豆瓣链接
中年版《伦敦生活》。
@潘誉晗：亚历克斯是一名文学经纪人，身为单身母亲的她把儿子鲁阿里抚养成人。现在，鲁阿里终于要上大学了，她打算开始崭新的生活，因为这天她突然意识到，已 50 岁的她不再年轻。她认定女性到了 60 岁无法性感，决定抓住这最后十年，拥抱新的恋情。只是她没想到，才上大学的鲁阿里退学回了家，父亲的病情也开始恶化。

作为莎朗·豪根「自传三部曲」的收官之作，真实而深刻的剧集，成功记录了一位女性迟来的青春期。夹在上有老下有中间的亚历克斯，就连崩溃也要挑时间。作为一名女儿和母亲，她被不顺遂的生活拉扯着，无法喘口气。可亚历克斯，又真的做好重新开始的准备了吗？荣格说「如果你的潜意识没有进入你的意识，那就是你的命运」，所以在没有真正意识到应该首先爱自己之前，亚历克斯自以为的做好准备，其实也只是自欺欺人而已。因为 50 岁的人生并不可悲，只要你想，依然可以性感。
[澳大利亚] 尘落
